divergences.summary: -f and -c accept a comma-separated list of positive integers, not ranges or open-ended selections
divergences.reason: A range needs an ordering and clamping model the streaming record profile does not yet declare. `cut -c2-4` is a usage error with status 2 rather than a silent approximation of GNU behavior.

divergences.summary: multi-field wc output is single-space separated instead of right-aligned in width-dependent columns
divergences.reason: GNU pads each count to a width derived from the largest input, which makes output depend on values the streaming profile never buffers. Single-field forms such as `wc -l` match exactly.

divergences.summary: diff always emits the unified format used by patch, with no context or ed output modes
divergences.reason: GNU diff defaults to the normal format and selects others by option. cf-vfs documents one format so `diff | patch` composes deterministically.

divergences.summary: type reports that a name is a function without printing its definition
divergences.reason: Bash re-renders the parsed function body, which would make `type` output depend on the formatter rather than on the profile. Reporting the classification keeps the output stable and is what a script testing for a function needs.

divergences.summary: printenv reports any set variable, not only exported ones
divergences.reason: A cf-vfs shell has one variable map and no separate process environment to hand a child, so `export` records intent rather than moving a value between scopes. `printenv NAME` therefore prints a variable a POSIX shell would keep to itself. Scripts that test for an inherited variable must not rely on the distinction.

divergences.summary: an executable file runs only as the cf-vfs shell profile, whatever its shebang names
divergences.reason: There is no process runtime to hand a file to, so the only interpreter that can exist is this shell. `/bin/sh`, `/bin/bash`, and `/usr/bin/env sh|bash` select it, a file with no shebang gets it, and every other interpreter is refused with status 126 rather than run by something it did not ask for. Interpreter arguments such as `#!/bin/sh -e` are refused for the same reason.

divergences.summary: a script sees every variable, function, and shell option of its caller, not only the exported ones
divergences.reason: A Bash script runs in a separate process and inherits only exported variables and no functions. There is no process boundary here and one variable map, so `export` records intent rather than moving a value; a child therefore sees unexported variables, the caller's functions, and options such as `set -e`. The isolation that does hold is outbound: nothing the child defines, and no working-directory change or `exit` it performs, reaches the caller. Do not rely on `export` to keep a value from a script.

divergences.summary: $- lists only the options this profile spells as short flags
divergences.reason: Bash also reports `h`, `B`, `c`, and interactivity flags for behavior that does not exist here — hashing, brace expansion, and a command-string invocation mode. Reporting `e` and `u` in a fixed order makes the value a declaration of what is on rather than an imitation of a flag set the runtime does not have.

divergences.summary: -r, -w, and -x report whether any class carries the bit, because there is no user to ask about
divergences.reason: A POSIX shell answers these for the effective user, so the same file gives different answers to different accounts and a privileged account can write a read-only file. There is no user, group, or account here and mode bits enforce nothing, so the predicate reports whether the bit is set for any class. That agrees with an unprivileged POSIX user, which the fixtures pin, and differs from a privileged one. It also does not consult the shell's read and write roots: those refuse the operation, and a predicate that reported them would conflate policy with metadata.

divergences.summary: an unquoted default such as ${X-~/d} keeps the tilde literal
divergences.reason: Tilde expansion runs on the written word, where quote provenance is still available. A default inside a parameter expansion is produced during that expansion, so treating it as a tilde prefix would mean re-scanning generated text as syntax — which is exactly what this runtime refuses to do everywhere else. Quoted `"${X-~/d}"` agrees with Bash; the unquoted form differs.

divergences.summary: patterns are a declared subset of POSIX basic and extended expressions; anything outside it is a usage error
divergences.reason: Patterns are parsed and matched by this project rather than handed to the JavaScript engine, so no JavaScript-only construct can mean something here that it does not mean in grep. The subset is literals, `.`, `*`, bracket expressions with ranges and POSIX classes, `^`, `$`, grouping, alternation, `+`, `?`, and intervals. Back-references, the GNU extensions `\\w`, `\\b`, `\\<`, and `\\>`, equivalence classes, and collating symbols are refused with status 2 rather than approximated, and `-i` folds the twenty-six ASCII pairs only, because the runtime declares LC_ALL=C.

divergences.summary: sed implements s, p, and d with addresses; the rest of the language is refused
divergences.reason: Hold space, branching, labels, and `a`, `i`, `c`, `y`, `r`, and `w` are a programming language rather than a utility, and several of them need state across records that a streaming profile cannot bound. Every command in the subset reads only the current record, so ordinary operation streams; `-i` is the one barrier and publishes a single guarded whole-file write. An unsupported command is status 2.

divergences.summary: alternation picks the first branch that matches rather than the longest, so `sed 's/a\\|ab/X/'` on `ab` gives `Xb` where GNU gives `X`
divergences.reason: Matching is a Thompson simulation, which is linear in the record however the pattern is written. A backtracking engine gives POSIX leftmost-longest more cheaply but has no bound: `grep 'a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*b'` against thirty-two characters takes seconds, and a synchronous match cannot be interrupted by the abort signal or the execution deadline, so one short pattern from a caller would burn the whole CPU limit. Bounded execution is the stronger requirement, and leftmost-first is the price. Whether a record matches at all is unaffected; only which text a group captures can differ.

divergences.summary: -p restores the mode and modification time of the named target only; entries beneath a recursive copy keep the time of the copy
divergences.reason: Restating every descendant would mean a second full walk of the subtree with one write per entry, which is unbounded work hidden behind a two-character option. The named target covers the ordinary use, and `find`-driven restatement covers the rest.

divergences.summary: ln requires -s; a hard link is a usage error rather than a copy
divergences.reason: A hard link needs an inode identity and a link count separate from the path, and this namespace has neither — an entry is its path. Making one silently copy would produce two files that agree until the first write and then diverge, which is worse than saying so. Status 2 with the reason named.

divergences.summary: a chain of more than forty links is refused with ELOOP even when it is not a cycle
divergences.reason: Linux uses the same bound for the same reason: a cycle cannot be told from deep nesting without one, and a constant makes the refusal deterministic rather than dependent on how much work the caller has already done. Resolution costs one indexed lookup per hop, so the bound is also what keeps a pathname from costing an unbounded number of queries.

divergences.summary: a link may name any path, including one outside the shell's roots; the refusal happens when it is followed
divergences.reason: Checking the target at creation would freeze the policy that was in force when the link was made, and a link is text rather than an access. Every read and write resolves the path first and checks the roots against what it resolved to, so a link out of the roots is created happily and refused with EACCES the moment anything follows it.

divergences.summary: a pattern whose literal prefix is a link expands normally, but a wildcard that would match a link name does not expand through it: `/li*/a.txt` finds nothing where `/link/a.txt` does
divergences.reason: A pattern is answered with one indexed range query against canonical paths, after canonicalizing the literal prefix. Expanding a wildcard through a link would mean globbing component by component and resolving each match before continuing, which turns one query into one per component per candidate — unbounded work for a pattern that is one character longer. The common forms (`/link/*`, and any pattern from a working directory reached through a link) resolve correctly.

divergences.summary: a trailing slash is normalized away by the shell, so `cat filelink/` reads the file and `rm -r dirlink/` removes the link
divergences.reason: Paths are canonical Unicode strings normalized once at the shell boundary, before any command sees them, which is what makes path handling uniform across every utility. The filesystem does honour a trailing slash — `stat` and the conditional predicates take the unnormalized form — but a command operand has already lost it. Making every operand carry the distinction would push path syntax into each utility rather than keeping it in one place.

divergences.summary: `link/..` names the directory holding the link, not the parent of what it points at
divergences.reason: Paths are normalized once, at the boundary, before anything is looked up — that is what makes `..` mean the same thing to every utility and keeps path handling out of each one. Resolving `..` against the target instead would mean interleaving normalization with lookups, so a path's meaning would depend on what happened to exist while it was being read. Bash's own `cd -L` behaves this way for the same reason.

divergences.command: cp, mv, rm, touch, mkdir, ln
divergences.summary: `/dev` and the names in it accept reads and writes but refuse every namespace change, so `cp /dev/null f`, `touch /dev/null`, and `rm /dev/null` are errors
divergences.reason: A device is a name the shell knows, not an entry. The alternative was letting the two views disagree — a real `/dev/null` would then be read as the device but listed, removed, and moved as a file, and a write to it would be silently discarded. One rule for every operation is worth losing the `cp /dev/null f` truncation idiom, which `> f` already spells.

divergences.summary: `/dev/stdin`, `/dev/stdout`, and `/dev/stderr` work as redirection sources and targets; as command operands they are a usage error
divergences.reason: A descriptor alias is a capability of the redirection layer, which holds this execution's streams. A command operand is a path, and this runtime has no file behind a descriptor for one to name. `< /dev/stdin` and `> /dev/stderr` are the supported spellings, and they compose the same way. `/dev/null` has no such restriction because it is not an alias.

divergences.summary: a redirection target that expands to other than one word fails with status 2, where Bash uses 1
divergences.reason: Redirection targets are resolved through the same expansion as any other word, and a field count that is not one is a usage error in this profile's status taxonomy: 2 is syntax and usage, 126 is policy, 127 is not found. Bash spends 1 on redirection failures generally. Brace expansion makes the case easy to write — `> f{1,2}` — so the difference is declared rather than left to be discovered.

cases.name: command-bypasses-a-function
cases.script:
PATH=/bin:/usr/bin
cat() { printf 'wrapped\n'; }
cat f.txt
command cat f.txt

cases.name: type-external-and-builtin
cases.script: PATH=/bin:/usr/bin; type cat; type cd; type echo
cases.stdout:
cat is /bin/cat
cd is a shell builtin
echo is a shell builtin

cases.name: printenv-named-values
cases.script: FIRST=one; SECOND=two; export FIRST SECOND; printenv FIRST SECOND

cases.name: script-scope-is-isolated
cases.script:
chmod 755 scope.sh
START=$PWD
V=parent
./scope.sh
printf '%s\n' "$V"
test "$PWD" = "$START" && printf 'cwd-kept\n'

cases.name: test-permission-predicates
cases.script:
chmod 400 perm.txt
test -r perm.txt && printf 'r'
test -w perm.txt || printf ' no-w'
test -x perm.txt || printf ' no-x'
chmod 755 perm.txt
test -x perm.txt && printf ' now-x'
printf '\n'

cases.name: test-size-predicate
cases.script:
test -s full.txt && printf 'full'
test -s empty.txt || printf ' empty'
printf '\n'

cases.name: chmod-symbolic-modes
cases.script:
chmod 600 m.txt; chmod +x m.txt; test -x m.txt && printf 'plus-x '
chmod 600 m.txt; chmod u+x m.txt; test -x m.txt && printf 'u-plus-x '
chmod 666 m.txt; chmod go-w m.txt; test -w m.txt && printf 'go-minus-w '
chmod 600 m.txt; chmod a=rx m.txt; test -x m.txt && printf 'a-equals-rx'
printf '\n'

cases.name: tilde-in-a-case-word
cases.script: HOME=/tmp/home; case ~ in /tmp/home) printf 'match\n';; *) printf 'no\n';; esac

cases.name: grep-quiet-status
cases.script: grep -q alpha in.txt; printf 'found=%s\n' "$?"; grep -q zzz in.txt; printf 'missing=%s\n' "$?"

cases.name: find-print0-through-xargs
cases.script: find t -type f -print0 | xargs -0 -n1 basename | sort

cases.name: ls-recursive
cases.stdout:
t:
a.txt
c.log
sub

t/sub:
b.txt

cases.name: expr-arithmetic-and-comparison
cases.script: expr 2 + 3; expr 7 / 2; expr 5 - 8; expr 1 = 1; expr abc = abc; expr length hello

cases.name: sed-line-numbers-span-operands
cases.script: sed -n '$p' f1.txt f2.txt; sed -n '1p' f1.txt f2.txt; sed -n '3p' f1.txt f2.txt

cases.name: grep-ignore-case-folds-bracket-members
cases.script: grep -i '[abc]' in.txt; grep -i '[ABC]' in.txt; grep -ic '[a-z0-9_-]' in.txt

cases.name: find-exec-semicolon-does-not-propagate-a-failure
cases.script: find t -name 'a.txt' -exec false {} ';' ; printf '%s' "$?"; find t -name 'a.txt' -exec false {} + ; printf '%s' "$?"

cases.name: ln-symbolic-creates-a-link-reported-as-itself
cases.script: ln -s real.txt link.txt; stat -c '%F' link.txt; stat -L -c '%F' link.txt; readlink link.txt; cat link.txt
cases.stdout:
symbolic link
regular file
real.txt
body

cases.name: ln-symbolic-stores-the-target-verbatim
cases.script: ln -s real.txt d/rel; ln -s /tmp/work/d/real.txt d/abs; readlink d/rel; readlink d/abs; cat d/rel; cat d/abs

cases.name: symlink-in-a-middle-component-is-followed
cases.script: ln -s t/sub dirlink; cat dirlink/deep.txt; readlink -f dirlink/deep.txt

cases.name: dangling-link-exists-but-does-not-resolve
cases.script: ln -s nowhere dangling; [ -L dangling ] && echo L-yes; [ -e dangling ] && echo e-yes || echo e-no; readlink dangling

cases.name: symlink-predicates-ask-about-the-link-or-the-target
cases.script: ln -s real.txt l; [ -L l ] && echo L; [ -h l ] && echo h; [ -f l ] && echo f; [ -e l ] && echo e; [ -L real.txt ] || echo plain-not-link

cases.name: find-reports-links-and-does-not-descend-into-one
cases.script: ln -s t dirlink; find t dirlink -type l | sort; find t dirlink -type f | sort; find dirlink | sort

cases.name: rm-removes-the-link-and-not-the-directory-it-names
cases.script: ln -s d dl; rm dl; ls d; if [ -e dl ]; then echo still-there; else echo link-gone; fi

cases.name: mv-renames-the-link-itself
cases.script: ln -s real.txt a; mv a b; stat -c '%F' b; readlink b; stat -c '%F' real.txt

cases.script: ln -s f.txt tree/l.txt; cp tree/l.txt flat.txt; stat -c '%F' flat.txt; cp -P tree/l.txt kept.txt; stat -c '%F' kept.txt; cp -r tree t2; stat -c '%F' t2/l.txt; readlink t2/l.txt
cases.stdout:
regular file
symbolic link
symbolic link
f.txt

cases.script: ln -s real.txt l; printf 'new\n' > l; cat real.txt; stat -c '%F' l

cases.script: ln -s real.txt l; if mkdir l 2>err.txt; then echo made; else echo refused; fi; stat -c '%F' l

cases.script: ln -s d dl; ls dl | sort; ls -d dl; ls -l dl | cut -c1

cases.script: ln -s d/real.txt l; readlink l; readlink -f l; readlink d/real.txt; printf 'rc=%s\n' "$?"

cases.name: a-link-chain-resolves-to-the-end
cases.script: ln -s real.txt one; ln -s one two; ln -s two three; cat three; readlink three; readlink -f three

cases.script: ln -s b a; ln -s a b; if cat a 2>err.txt; then echo read; else echo loop-refused; fi; [ -L a ] && echo still-a-link
